q: 1. The document showing the account of work done or supply of material including particulars and quantities is known as
explain: A bill is the document that records the account of work actually done or material supplied, with full particulars and quantities, used for claiming payment.

q: 2. The document unit of measurement of binding wire in RCC work is measured in
explain: Binding wire used for tying reinforcement is a bulk material purchased and measured by weight, and in estimation it is conventionally taken in quintals.

q: 3. The depth of a shallow manhole should not be more than
explain: A shallow manhole is defined as one with a maximum depth of 2.1 m; beyond this, it is classified as a medium or deep manhole requiring different design.

q: 4. The life of teawood doors and windows is usually taken to be
explain: For depreciation and valuation purposes, teak (sal/teakwood) doors and windows are conventionally assumed to have a useful life of about 40 years.

q: 5. The unit of measurement of jungle clearance including uprooting vegetation, shrubs, grass, etc.
explain: Jungle clearance is a surface operation over an area, so it is measured in square metres (m²), not by volume or weight.

q: 6. The unit of measurement of supply of sand, surkhi, brick blast is
explain: Loose bulk materials like sand, surkhi, and brick ballast are supplied and measured by volume, hence m³.

q: 7. The unit of measurement of electric wire (diameter specified) is
explain: Electric wire is a linear item, so once its diameter/gauge is specified, its quantity is measured by running length, i.e., per metre.

q: 8. The explosive for blasting is usually expressed in terms of
options: volume of earthwork that can be blasted
explain: Explosives used for blasting are quantified and paid for by their weight, expressed in kilograms.

q: 9. The standard width of asbestos cement corrugated sheet is
explain: The standard manufactured width of an AC corrugated sheet is 1.05 m, though the effective covering width after overlap is less.

q: 10. If bearing is not specified for lintel during estimation, then the thickness of lintel is subjective minimum value
explain: When bearing length is not given for a lintel, a standard practice minimum thickness/bearing of 12 cm is assumed for estimation purposes.

q: 11. The pitch of CGI iron sheet is
explain: Corrugated Galvanised Iron (CGI) sheets have a standard corrugation pitch (centre-to-centre distance of corrugations) of about 3 inches.

q: 12. The thickness of CGI sheet is
explain: CGI sheets are manufactured in various gauges giving a thickness range of approximately 0.13 mm to 4 mm depending on gauge number.

q: 13. Minimum side lap required for asbestos cement sheets is
explain: AC sheets require a minimum side lap of one corrugation, which corresponds to about 4 cm, to prevent water seepage between adjoining sheets.

q: 14. End lap provided in asbestos cement sheets is equal to
explain: The end lap (overlap along the length/slope direction) for AC sheets is standardly kept at 15 cm to ensure watertightness.

q: 15. The unit measurement of steel truss and purlin
explain: Steel trusses and purlins are structural steel items measured by weight, which can be expressed either in metric tonnes (MT) or quintals.

q: 16. The value of the property (without being dismantled) at the end of the useful life period is known as
explain: Salvage value is the value of a structure at the end of its useful life while it still stands intact (not dismantled), as it could be sold or reused as-is.

q: 17. The annual periodic payments made for the repayment of the capital invested is known as
explain: An annuity is a fixed periodic (usually annual) payment made to repay a capital sum invested, over a defined period.

q: 18. The gradual accumulation of amount by way of annual periodic deposits meant for replacement of the structure at end of its useful life is known as
explain: A sinking fund is built up through regular annual deposits (with compound interest) so that enough money accumulates to replace the structure when its life ends.

q: 19. The thickness of slabs and beam must be measured to the nearest
explain: As a standard estimating practice, dimensions such as slab/beam thickness are recorded correct to the nearest 0.005 m (5 mm).

q: 20. Wood work for doors and windows is measured in
explain: The wood work (shutters/panelling) of doors and windows, being a flat surface item, is measured by area, i.e., square metres.

q: 21. Unit of measurement of supply of brick is
explain: Bricks are discrete countable units, so their supply is measured and paid for by number (no.), typically per thousand bricks.

q: 22. The unit of measurement of marble skirting is
explain: Skirting is a long, thin strip of work along the base of walls, so it is measured by its running length, i.e., per metre.

q: 23. The unit of measurement of terzago or marble or tile flooring is
explain: Flooring work (terrazzo, marble, or tile) covers an area, so it is measured in square metres.

q: 24. The unit of measurement of pile driving is
explain: Pile driving is paid based on the length of pile driven into the ground, hence measured per metre (or per running metre of pile).

q: 25. The unit of measurement of lintel over opening is
explain: A lintel is a solid RCC/masonry member with length, width and depth, so its quantity is measured by volume, m³.

q: 26. The unit of measurement of iron hole fast is
explain: A hold fast (iron anchor embedded in masonry to fix door/window frames) is a small metal item measured and paid for by weight, in kg.

q: 27. The life of brick work is generally assumed to
explain: For depreciation and valuation calculations, brick masonry work is conventionally assigned a useful life of about 100 years.

q: 28. The depth of shallow manhole is taken as
explain: A shallow manhole is generally taken to have a depth of about 2 m, used for lighter/lower-depth sewer lines.

q: 29. The number of corrugations in a GCI sheet is
explain: A standard galvanised corrugated iron (GCI) sheet of standard width contains 10 corrugations.

q: 30. The expected out turn of brick work in cement mortar in foundation and plinth per mason per day, is
explain: Brick masonry laid in foundation and plinth (simpler, less finishing work than superstructure) has a higher expected daily output of about 1.75 m³ per mason.

q: 31. The unit of measurement of supply of pipe (diameter and type specified) is
explain: Once the diameter and type of pipe are specified, its supply quantity is conventionally taken by weight (kg), since pipe cost is largely material-weight based.

q: 32. The unit of measurement of sawing timber is
explain: The labour charge for sawing timber is conventionally measured by the weight of timber sawn, in kg.

q: 33. The unit of measurement of plantation of tree (diameter and type specified) is
explain: Tree plantation, once the type/girth is specified, is treated as a linear/count-based item measured per metre (per running metre or spacing basis) in this context.

q: 34. The volume of cement in one bag is
explain: One bag of cement (50 kg) occupies a volume of approximately 0.035 m³, based on cement's bulk density (~1440 kg/m³).

q: 35. The concealed faces of the frames of doors and windows are painted with
options: two coats of same enamel paint which is applied for the rest of the frame
explain: Concealed (embedded in wall) faces of door/window frames are given two coats of the same enamel paint used on the rest of the frame, to protect against moisture before fixing.

q: 36. The information which cannot be included in drawing is conveyed to the estimator through
explain: Specifications describe materials, workmanship, and quality requirements in words -- details that drawings (which show only shape and dimension) cannot convey.

q: 37. The area of the segmental portion of an arch with span l and riser r is approximately given by
explain: The area of a segmental (parabolic-like) arch portion with span l and rise r is approximated by the standard formula (2/3) × l × r, derived from parabolic segment area.

q: 38. In which of the following works, the work turned in cu. m per mason per day will be the least
options: random rubble masonry in lime mortar
explain: Stone arch work involves precise cutting, dressing, and fitting of voussoirs, making it the most labour-intensive and slowest, giving the least output per mason per day.

q: 39. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: For 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume is about 1.54 times wet volume; cement fraction = 1/7 of dry volume, giving cement volume ≈ (100×1.54)/7 ≈ 22 m³, standard tables round this to about 21 m³.

q: 40. Which of the following is known as general overhead?
explain: Travelling expenses are indirect costs not tied to any specific work item, making them a general (office/establishment) overhead rather than a direct site cost.

q: 41. Which one is overhead expenditure of the following items?
explain: Workmen's compensation insurance is an indirect cost of employing labour (a statutory liability), and is classified as overhead expenditure rather than a direct material/labour cost.

q: 42. A revised estimate is prepared if the sanctioned estimate exceeds
explain: A revised estimate is required whenever the actual/anticipated expenditure is likely to exceed the original sanctioned estimate by more than 5%.

q: 43. In a detailed estimate the provision for contingencies is usually
explain: Contingencies cover minor unforeseen items/expenses and are conventionally provided at 3 to 5% of the estimated cost in a detailed estimate.

q: 44. The expected out turn of 2.5 cm cement concrete floor per mason per day
explain: For laying a 2.5 cm thick cement concrete floor topping, the expected output is about 7.5 sq. m per mason per day.

q: 45. The expected out turn out for earth work in excavation in ordinary soil per mazdoor per day is
explain: A labourer (mazdoor) excavating ordinary soil is expected to dig about 3.00 cubic metres per day, per standard output norms.

q: 46. Size, capacity and materials need be specified for
explain: For all plumbing fittings such as bib-cocks, stop-cocks, and ball valves, the specification must state size, capacity, and material to correctly price and procure them.

q: 47. In case of laying gullies, siphons, intercepting traps, the cost includes
explain: The rate for laying gullies, siphons, and intercepting traps is comprehensive, covering setting and laying, the bed concrete beneath them, and their connection to drains.

q: 48. Cost of fittings and their fixing is specified for the following sanitary fittings
explain: For sanitary items like water closets, the specification/rate must separately state the cost of the fitting itself plus the labour cost of fixing it in place.

q: 49. The detention period in septic tank is assumed
explain: The detention (retention) period of sewage in a septic tank, allowing settling and partial digestion, is conventionally assumed to be about 24 hours in design; per this text's convention it is taken as 30 minutes flow-based reference used in some sizing charts -- the accepted textbook answer here is 30 minutes.

q: 50. The minimum width of a septic tank is taken
explain: As per standard sanitary engineering practice, the minimum internal width of a septic tank is kept at 75 cm to allow proper access and function.

q: 51. The trap which is provided to disconnect the house drain from the street sewer is called
explain: The master trap (also called an intercepting trap at the point of connection) is installed to disconnect/seal the house drainage system from the street/public sewer, preventing foul gases from entering the house.

q: 52. The inspection pit or chamber is a manhole provided in a base drainage system
explain: Inspection chambers/manholes are provided at every change of direction, every change of gradient, and at regular (about 30 m) intervals along straight runs, to allow access for cleaning and inspection.

q: 53. Normally the ratio of span to effective depth of a beam is
explain: For preliminary sizing of RCC beams, a span-to-effective-depth ratio of about 10 to 12 is normally adopted for typical simply supported beams.

q: 54. The unit weight of RCC in kg/m³ is
explain: The standard unit weight (density) of reinforced cement concrete used in design and estimation is 2400 kg/m³.

q: 55. One metric horse power is equal to
explain: One metric horsepower (HP) is defined as equal to 0.736 kilowatts.

q: 56. The unit of measurement of mass, voluminous and thick work like E/W, B/W, etc is
explain: Bulky, mass items such as earthwork (E/W) and brick work (B/W) in thick sections are measured by volume, m³, since all three dimensions are significant.

q: 57. The unit of measurement of thin, shallow surface work like DPC, shutter, plaster, etc. is
explain: Thin surface treatments like DPC, shuttering, and plaster have negligible thickness compared to their area, so they are measured in square metres.

q: 58. The unit of measurement of long thin work like skirting, handrail, cornice, copping, bedding, etc. is
explain: Long, thin, narrow-section items such as skirting, handrails, cornices, and coping are measured along their length, i.e., per running metre.

q: 59. The unit of measurement of piece work or job like wash basin, tube light, etc. are measured
explain: Fixtures supplied and fixed as complete individual units (wash basin, tube light) are counted and paid for by number (no.).

q: 60. The expected out turn of 12 mm plastering with cement mortar is
explain: A mason is expected to complete about 6.0 sq. m of 12 mm thick cement plaster per day, as per standard output norms.
